summary: Explains how RSVP-TE signaling can link a restoration path to a failed one in GMPLS end-to-end recovery. It covers the case where the failed path is kept reserved rather than torn down, as well as resource sharing and reverting traffic to the original path. It reviews existing procedures and needs no new protocol extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: If a road is closed, you take a detour but keep the old road saved for you until it reopens. This explains how the signs tell everyone about both roads.

questions: make before break vs make while break
subtitle: How RSVP-TE signaling keeps failed paths reserved while a restoration path is set up, shares resources, and reverts traffic afterwards.

tldr.problem: In non-packet transport networks, providers want to keep the resources of a failed working or protecting path reserved after a failure, so traffic can revert to the preferred path once the failure is repaired.
tldr.mechanism: A restoration LSP is signaled with an ASSOCIATION object of type Recovery, shares resources with the LSPs it restores, and reversion is done by either make-while-break or make-before-break.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is informative and defines no new RSVP-TE extensions. It reviews procedures from RFC 3209, RFC 4872, RFC 4873 and RFC 6689.

today: RFC 8131 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It reviews existing procedures and defines no new protocol.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
GMPLS extends MPLS to set up Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in non-packet transport networks, including Time Division Multiplexing, Lambda Switching and Fiber Switching. RSVP-TE has been extended for recovery schemes such as end-to-end recovery (RFC 4872) and segment recovery (RFC 4873). RFC 6689 describes using an ASSOCIATION object in the RSVP Path message with the type Recovery to identify LSPs for restoration, and the type Resource Sharing to identify LSPs that share resources.

End-to-end schemes usually set up the restoration LSP after a failure is detected. In revertive schemes the working and/or protecting LSP are not torn down in the control plane. Providers want their resources kept reserved so service can revert to the preferred path for deterministic behavior and a guaranteed SLA. The RFC says it is strictly informative and defines no RSVP-TE extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone and fiber networks sometimes need to reroute when something breaks. This RFC explains how to reroute while saving the original route for later.

sections.title: Restoration Schemes
sections.content:
In 1+R restoration, a working LSP is pre-established. After a failure is detected and notified, a second LSP is established as a restoration LSP. Unlike a protecting LSP, which is set up before the failure, a restoration LSP is set up when needed. Working resources are generally not released, so both LSPs coexist and can share resources. When the failure is repaired, the restoration LSP is torn down as traffic reverts.

In 1+1+R, both a working and a protecting LSP are pre-established, and a restoration LSP is set up after the failure of either or both. The RFC lists models with one restoration LSP at a time and variants with two restoration LSPs, one for working and one for protecting. If a restoration LSP also fails, it is torn down and a new one is set up.
sections.plainLanguage: 1+R is having a main road and building a detour only when needed. 1+1+R has a main road and a backup road ready, and builds a third detour if both break.

sections.title: Association and Resource Sharing
sections.content:
To keep failed LSPs reserved, the restoration LSP is signaled with an ASSOCIATION object whose type is Recovery, and whose Association ID and Association Source are copied from the LSP it restores. A restoration LSP for a working LSP clears the P bit in the PROTECTION object, while one for a protecting LSP sets it.

LSPs can share resources if they set the Shared Explicit (SE) flag in SESSION_ATTRIBUTE and either have identical SESSION objects (RFC 3209) or matching ASSOCIATION objects of type Resource Sharing (RFC 6689), which allows different SESSION objects.

Because a cross-connection cannot connect a shared resource to two different resources at once, node behavior depends on how much is reused. Interrupted traffic is already affected by the failure, so reconfiguring cross-connections during restoration does not further impact it.
sections.plainLanguage: The new detour carries a note saying which broken road it replaces. Roads that share a piece of pavement have to agree who is using it.

sections.title: What Each Node Does
sections.content:
The RFC divides nodes into three categories during restoration LSP setup. A node that reuses existing resources on both its input and output interfaces just reserves them and needs no cross-connection command. A node that reuses an existing resource on only one interface reserves resources and sends a reconfiguration cross-connection command for the interface where new resources are needed. A node that uses new resources on both interfaces reserves them and sends cross-connection commands for both.

This differs from normal LSP setup, because some nodes do not reconfigure the cross-connection, and deciding whether to send a command depends on checking whether LSPs share resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Some stops on the detour are already on the old road and need nothing. Some need one new switch flipped. Some are brand new and need both flipped.

sections.title: Reverting to the Original Path
sections.content:
After the failure is repaired, traffic can revert from the restoration LSP in two ways. In make-while-break the head-end simply deletes the restoration LSP, and as reservations are removed the data plane reverts to the working or protecting LSP's reservations. It is simple but has limits: no rollback if reconfiguration fails, no completion guarantee because deletion may be partial (soft state is not useful in these networks), and no explicit completion notice to the head-end.

In make-before-break the head-end first establishes a new reversion LSP that duplicates the working or protecting LSP configuration, with identical ASSOCIATION and PROTECTION objects. Only if it is set up successfully are the original and restoration LSPs deleted. This gives rollback (the restoration LSP is still there if the make step fails), a completion guarantee (Path and Resv messages are refreshed), and notification (the head-end gets a Resv message for the reversion LSP).

Both methods cause some traffic disruption when cross-connections must be reconfigured on shared resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching back can be done by closing the detour and hoping the old road is ready, or by first checking the old road works and only then closing the detour. The second way is safer.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC reviews procedures from RFC 3209, RFC 4872, RFC 4873 and RFC 6689, and defines no new procedures. It says it introduces no new security issues beyond those already covered in those documents. It requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is invented here, so nothing new needs to be guarded.
